title: Title I Reading Corner October Newsletter
source_title: Marshall E-News | Smore Newsletters for Education

blocks.content:
READING 

CORNER READING CORNER

Title I Reading Corner October Newsletter How Important is the Alphabet? The alphabet is very important! The alphabet is the foundation or building block for reading, writing, and spelling. It is important for each child to recognize and name all the letters and combinations of letters in and out of order and also the sounds associated with them, to be successful with literacy.In Kindergarten, students are taught the letter sounds in conjunction with the letter names. For example, a teacher might say, “Today we are learning the letter that says /b/. What are some words that have the /b/ sound? This is the letter that spells the /b/ sound. It is called the letter b. This is how we make the letter b.” It helps students to connect sounds to known words, as this helps develop a memory aid.As students begin to recognize the letters and understand their sounds, they are able to begin reading and writing independently. This emergent reading begins in Kindergarten (or preschool) and continues through the elementary school years.  It is also important for early learners to know the symbols or ways we write the letters or combinations of letters or graphemes that represent sounds. A combination of 1,2,3, or 4 graphemes can represent a phoneme or sound. For example: 1 letter p, 2 letters ch, 3 letters igh, 4 letters tion. Recognizing letters, sounds, and combinations of letters and sounds is a skill that is needed to read unfamiliar words independently. As students progress in their knowledge of the alphabet and phonics, they are directly and explicitly taught the more advanced letter-sound relationships in a progression from least difficult to more difficult. This instruction continues through the early elementary years. What can I do to help my student?Read to/and with your child every dayRequest a copy of alphabet flash cardsMatching games for uppercase and lowercase lettersCar games could include saying a word, and your child has to tell you what the beginning sound of the word is, then progress to ending sounds. The ultimate goal is that your child can tell you all the sounds in the word.

summary: The **Title I Reading Corner** newsletter explains the importance of alphabet knowledge as the foundation for reading, writing, and spelling. Students learn letter names, sounds, and graphemes (letter combinations) progressively from Kindergarten through elementary years. **Parents can help** by reading with their child daily, using alphabet flash cards, playing matching games with uppercase/lowercase letters, and playing car games that identify beginning, ending, and all sounds in words.

title: Volunteer and Visitor Policy Requirements
source_title: Marshall E-News | Smore Newsletters for Education

blocks.content:
VOLUNTEER 

& 

VISITOR 

POLICY VOLUNTEER & VISITOR POLICY

As we continue with our volunteer policy this year, please remember that any adult volunteer who wishes to enter the school building must have a volunteer application on file with the office every school year. After a parent’s second visit to the building, they are required to complete fingerprinting and a background check through the Central Registration Office. Please plan to complete this process at least 3 weeks prior to the event. This allows adequate time for the background check to be completed and for the appropriate information to be provided to the school administrator for planning purposes. Once completed, your background check is valid for 5 years.Central Registration Office:Ruth Michael📞 513-273-3101We appreciate your understanding and cooperation as we work to keep our students, staff, and school community safe. Public schools have implemented these regulations to comply with state and federal safety requirements regarding volunteers and visitors in schools.
